1.tip: RTP = Real-Time: things you watch or hear live, video and voice.
1.why: RTP carries live media that must arrive on time, like voice calls and video streams. Web pages and file transfers can wait, so they use TCP instead.

2.tip: ZigBee buzzes around the smart home: low power, low data rate.
2.why: ZigBee is built for small smart home devices like lights and sensors that send tiny amounts of data and must save battery. LoRaWAN is for long range, 5G and Wi-Fi for high speed.

3.cue: route to forward messages through an internetwork
3.tip: Internet layer = IP = routing between networks.
3.why: The internet layer of TCP/IP is where IP lives. It adds addresses and picks paths so packets can travel across many networks.

4.cue: record types A, NS, AAAA, MX
4.tip: A, AAAA, NS, MX are DNS records: name to address, name server, mail exchanger.
4.why: DNS servers store records: A for IPv4 addresses, AAAA for IPv6, NS for name servers and MX for mail servers. They answer name lookups with these.

5.tip: Proprietary = property: one owner controls it.
5.why: A proprietary protocol belongs to one company, which decides how it works and who may use it. Open protocols can be used freely by anyone.

6.tip: DNS is the phone book of the internet: names to numbers.
6.why: DNS turns a name you can remember, like cisco.com, into the IP address your computer needs to reach the server.

7.why: Well-known port 110 belongs to POP3, which clients use to download email. SMTP is 25, DNS is 53, DHCP is 67/68.

8.cue: Windows PC, see the IP configuration
8.tip: IP CONFIG = IP configuration. The show commands are for Cisco devices.
8.why: On Windows, ipconfig shows the PC's IP address, mask and default gateway. The show commands run on Cisco routers and switches, not Windows.

9.tip: No dedicated server, just one PC sharing with its peers = P2P.
9.why: Each home computer acts as both client and server, sharing its printer directly. With no dedicated server, this is a peer-to-peer network.

10.tip: Virus = bad code running on your device, like a germ in your body.
10.why: A virus is malicious code that runs on an end device and spreads by attaching to other files. Filtering devices are firewalls, and crashing a service is DoS.

keys.k: audio conference, financial transactions, web page

11.tip: Live first, money second, browsing last.
11.why: Live audio breaks if delayed, so it gets top priority. Financial transactions matter to the business, so they come next. Reading a web page can wait.

12.cue: Host1 transfer a file to the server, layers

keys.k: application, transport, Internet, and network access layers

12.tip: The end host uses all 4 TCP/IP layers. Session and data link are OSI names, not TCP/IP.
12.why: A file transfer starts at the application, is split into segments at transport, gets IP addresses at internet, and is framed at network access. The host uses all four TCP/IP layers.

13.cue: default gateway setting of host H1
13.tip: Gateway = the router port on YOUR LAN, the nearest door out.
13.why: The default gateway is the router interface on the same LAN as the host. For H1 that is R1's G0/0. Serial ports connect routers to each other, not to hosts.

14.cue: service is provided by Internet Messenger
14.tip: Messenger = messages = live chat between people.
14.why: Instant messaging apps let remote users send text back and forth in real time. Remote access to devices is Telnet or SSH, and name lookups are DNS.

15.cue: building the table that is shown
15.tip: IP address next to MAC address = ARP table.
15.why: The table pairs IP addresses with MAC addresses. ARP builds it by asking 'who has this IP?' and saving the MAC address in the reply.

16.tip: Lights and motors make noise: EMI (electromagnetic) and RFI (radio frequency).
16.why: Fluorescent lights and electric equipment give off electromagnetic and radio noise that leaks into copper wires. Crosstalk comes from nearby wires, attenuation from length.

17.cue: remote LAN segment, no mappings in its ARP cache

keys.k: MAC address of the default gateway

17.tip: Remote target? ARP for the GATEWAY, not the far host.
17.why: A frame only travels on the local LAN. For a remote destination the host sends the frame to its router, so it ARPs for the default gateway's MAC address.

18.why: Port 53 is the well-known port for DNS name lookups. POP3 is 110 and IMAP is 143.

19.tip: Find the smallest power of 2 above hosts+2: 32. /27 = .224 gives 30 hosts.
19.why: You need 25 hosts plus a network and broadcast address. A /27 (255.255.255.224) has 32 addresses, 30 usable, which fits. A /28 has only 14 usable.

20.tip: Trojan horse: a gift that hides bad code inside.
20.why: A Trojan horse is malicious code that pretends to be a useful program. Once it runs on your device, it does harm in the background.

21.tip: HTTPS = HTTP + S for Secure: the web, encrypted. SSH is the secure remote access one.
21.why: HTTPS is the web protocol HTTP with encryption added, so pages, pictures and video travel privately. Secure remote access to devices is SSH.

22.cue: keep track of the data flow between multiple application sessions
22.tip: IP address finds the PC. Port number finds the app.
22.why: Every app on the PC uses its own source port number. Replies come back to that port, so the PC knows which app gets each packet. IP and MAC are the same for all apps.

23.tip: 61 + 2 = 63, next power of 2 is 64. /26 = .192 gives 62 hosts.
23.why: A /26 (255.255.255.192) gives 64 addresses, 62 usable, which fits 61 devices. A /27 only gives 30 usable.

24.tip: DoS = Denial of Service: nobody gets served.
24.why: A denial of service attack floods or breaks a device or service so it slows down or crashes, and real users can't use it.

keys.k: send email to a mail server

25.tip: SMTP = Send Mail To People. It sends, POP and IMAP fetch.
25.why: SMTP is used to send email: from your client to the mail server, and from one mail server to another. Getting mail to read is POP3 or IMAP.

26.cue: function provided by the transport layer
26.tip: Two browser windows = two source ports. Transport sorts which data goes to which window.
26.why: Each browser window uses its own source port, so the transport layer can send each page back to the right window. A burned-in ID is a MAC address, and screen formatting is the presentation job.

27.tip: Attenuation = attention fades the farther you go: signal gets weaker with distance.
27.why: Attenuation means a signal loses strength as it travels farther along the media. Leakage between pairs is crosstalk, and travel time is latency.

28.tip: Ladder: > user EXEC, enable, # privileged EXEC, then conf t.
28.why: The Switch> prompt means user EXEC mode, where configure terminal isn't allowed. You must type enable to get to privileged EXEC (#) first.

29.cue: top layer of the TCP/IP protocol suite
29.tip: Top layer = application. POP and DNS are apps; TCP/UDP transport, IP internet, Ethernet bottom.
29.why: The top TCP/IP layer is the application layer, where POP and DNS work. TCP and UDP are transport, IP is internet and Ethernet is network access.

30.tip: Authentication = who you are. Authorization = what you may do. Accounting = what you did.
30.why: Deciding that some users can only read while admins can edit is about permissions. In AAA, permissions are authorization.

31.cue: requirements defined by the protocols, message transmission
31.tip: Protocols set the message: how big, how coded, how delivered. Cables and installs are hardware, not protocol rules.
31.why: Protocols define rules for the message itself: its size, how it is encoded, and delivery like unicast, multicast or broadcast. Connectors and media are physical choices.

keys.k: does not require a dedicated end-to-end connection
operates independently of the network media

32.tip: IP is connectionless, best effort and media independent. Reliability is TCP's job.
32.why: IP sends each packet without setting up a connection first and works over any media, copper, fiber or wireless. It doesn't retransmit, reorder or guarantee delivery: TCP does that.

33.tip: Login = security, good video = QoS, backup link = fault tolerance.
33.why: The username and password show security. Keeping the video excellent is QoS. The backup ISP link taking over without anyone noticing is fault tolerance.

34.cue: signal degradation when using UTP cabling
34.tip: UTP is Unshielded, so shielding can't be the issue. Light loss is fiber.
34.why: Badly attached connectors and cheap cable or connectors let noise in and weaken the signal. UTP has no shield, and loss of light only happens in fiber.

35.tip: /26 from .64 runs .64 to .127, and .96 sits in the middle.
35.why: 192.168.1.64/26 covers .64 to .127, with .65 to .126 usable, so .96 fits. The /27, /28 and /29 choices end before .96 (at .63, .47 and .71).

36.cue: which two statements about network connectivity
36.tip: Trace finished = connected. Count the lines = hops.
36.why: The output reaches 192.168.100.1, so there is connectivity, and it lists four hops on the way. A reply that arrives proves the gateway works too.

37.cue: assess traffic flow patterns, protocol analyzer
37.tip: Capture when it's busy, and in more than one place.
37.why: Capturing at busy times shows real traffic, and capturing on several segments shows the whole network. Weekends or one area alone would give a misleading picture.

38.tip: ipv6 unicast-routing turns the router into an IPv6 router, and routers send RAs.
38.why: This command makes the device act as an IPv6 router. IPv6 routers announce themselves with ICMPv6 Router Advertisements so hosts can learn the prefix and gateway.

39.cue: OSI layers map to the application layer of TCP/IP
39.tip: Top three OSI layers (7, 6, 5: All People Seem) = TCP/IP application.
39.why: TCP/IP squeezes the top three OSI layers, application, presentation and session, into one application layer. Transport stays its own layer.

40.cue: Ethernet frame header attached by PC1
40.tip: Routers strip the old frame and put on a new one for each link.
40.why: A Layer 2 header only works on one link. R1 removes the Ethernet header and builds a new header for the serial link S0/0/0 before sending the packet on.

41.cue: default gateway address is incorrectly configured
41.tip: Wrong gateway = stuck at home. Local works, remote fails.
41.why: The default gateway is only used for traffic leaving the local network. With a wrong gateway, the host still talks to local devices but can't reach hosts on other networks.

42.tip: ARP request is a broadcast, the owner of the IP answers with a reply.
42.why: When a host knows the IP but not the MAC, it broadcasts an ARP request to the whole LAN. Only the device with that IP sends back a unicast ARP reply with its MAC.

43.tip: 90 + 2 = 92, next power of 2 is 128. /25 = .128 gives 126 hosts.
43.why: A /25 (255.255.255.128) has 128 addresses, 126 usable, which fits 90 devices. A /26 would only give 62.

44.cue: ICMPv6 messages not present in ICMP for IPv4
44.tip: Neighbor and Router messages (NDP) are new in IPv6. Unreachable and Time Exceeded exist in both.
44.why: IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery messages like Neighbor Solicitation and Router Advertisement in place of ARP and other tasks. Destination Unreachable and Time Exceeded also exist in IPv4.

45.why: Port 80 is the well-known port for web traffic using HTTP.

46.cue: advantage of adopting IMAP instead of POP

keys.k: kept in the mail servers until they are manually deleted

46.tip: IMAP keeps mail on the server. POP pops it off to your device.
46.why: With IMAP, email stays on the server until you delete it, so you can see it from any device and it's backed up in one place. POP usually downloads and removes it.

47.cue: ping the IP address but cannot ping the URL
47.tip: IP works but name fails? It's DNS. nslookup = name server lookup.
47.why: If the IP works but the name doesn't, name resolution is the problem. nslookup tests DNS lookups directly.

keys.k: enables IPv4 and IPv6 to utilize the same physical medium

48.tip: LLC talks UP to the network layer. MAC talks DOWN to the media.
48.why: LLC is the upper data link sublayer. It marks which network layer protocol is inside the frame, so IPv4 and IPv6 can share the same wire. CSMA/CD and frame fields are MAC jobs.

keys.k: upper layer networking software and Ethernet NIC hardware

49.tip: LLC = the link between software above and NIC hardware below. MAC addresses and FCS are MAC sublayer.
49.why: LLC connects the network software to the NIC and adds control info about the protocol inside. MAC addresses, frame structure and the FCS trailer belong to the MAC sublayer.

50.tip: LLC labels what's inside. MAC handles addresses and media access.
50.why: LLC adds control information that says which network layer protocol is carried, like IPv4 or IPv6. Applying MAC addresses and CSMA/CD are MAC sublayer tasks.

keys.k: enables IPv4 and IPv6 to utilize the same physical medium

51.tip: LLC = label the protocol so many can share. MAC = addresses, structure, FCS.
51.why: LLC adds control info that names the network protocol, which lets IPv4 and IPv6 share the same media. MAC addresses, frame structure and the FCS trailer are MAC sublayer jobs.

keys.k: enables IPv4 and IPv6 to utilize the same physical medium
upper layer networking software and Ethernet NIC hardware

52.tip: LLC sits between software and NIC. MAC does addressing and frame structure.
52.why: LLC links the network software to the NIC hardware and lets several network protocols like IPv4 and IPv6 share one medium. Addresses and frame structure are MAC sublayer jobs.

53.tip: Switch gateway = a way home for its replies. Without it, you can only manage it from the same subnet.
53.why: A Layer 2 switch needs a default gateway to send replies to other networks. With it set, an admin on a different network can reach the switch with SSH or Telnet.

54.tip: SSH = Secure SHell. "transport input ssh" lets only encrypted logins in, no Telnet.
54.why: This command allows only SSH on the vty lines, so remote sessions are encrypted. Telnet, which sends everything in plain text, is blocked.

55.cue: free wireless networking tools to determine information
55.why: Gathering information about a network to plan an attack later is reconnaissance. Nothing has been broken into or crashed yet.

keys.k: basic set of rules for exchanging

56.tip: HTTP = the basic web rules. Add S for secure (HTTPS).
56.why: HTTP is the set of rules browsers and web servers use to exchange text, pictures, sound and video. It has no encryption; that's HTTPS.

57.tip: 67/68 = DHCP server/client. Think 'DHCP hands out addresses at 67'.
57.why: UDP port 67 is the DHCP server port, used when a client asks for an IP address. FTP is 20/21, SSH 22, Telnet 23.

58.cue: large number of ARP request and reply messages
58.tip: ARP requests are broadcasts: they flood everywhere and everyone must read them.
58.why: ARP requests are broadcasts, so they go to every device on the subnet and each one has to stop and process them. Too many can slow the whole LAN.

59.cue: confirm the IP address and DNS configurations
59.tip: ipconfig = my settings, ping = reach the router, nslookup = test DNS.
59.why: ipconfig shows the PC's IP and DNS settings, ping tests reaching the local router, and nslookup checks that DNS works.

keys.k: switch the packet to the directly connected interface

60.tip: Directly connected = no next hop needed. Just send it out that port.
60.why: If the destination is on a network attached to the router, there is no next hop to look up. The router simply sends the packet out that interface.

keys.k: protect end devices from becoming infected

61.tip: Anti-spyware lives on your PC and keeps bad software out.
61.why: Antispyware is software on your own device that blocks and removes malicious programs that spy on you. Filtering traffic is a firewall, and secure tunnels are VPNs.

62.cue: user ID, password, and session contents private
62.tip: SSH = Secure SHell. Telnet sends everything in plain text.
62.why: SSH encrypts the login and everything you type over the network. Telnet sends it all in clear text, and console or AUX need a cable at the device.

63.cue: most effective ways to defend against malware
63.tip: Patch it and protect it: updates plus antivirus.
63.why: Updates fix the security holes that malware uses, and antivirus finds and removes malware. VPNs, RAID and passwords protect other things.

64.cue: spreadsheet add-on disables the local software firewall
64.tip: A useful-looking add-on that secretly does harm = Trojan horse.
64.why: The add-on looks like a helpful tool but secretly turns off the firewall. Hidden harm inside something useful is a Trojan horse.

65.cue: ensure that a transmitted data signal has not been altered
65.tip: FCS = Frame Check Sequence, the trailer that checks the frame.
65.why: The sender calculates a value (a CRC) from the frame and puts it in the FCS trailer. The receiver does the same math, and if the numbers differ, the frame was damaged.

66.tip: 4 + 2 = 6, next power of 2 is 8. /29 = .248 gives 6 hosts.
66.why: A /29 (255.255.255.248) has 8 addresses, 6 usable, which fits 4 devices. The other masks waste many more addresses.

keys.k: Retrieves email from the server by downloading

67.tip: POP3 pops your mail down to your device.
67.why: POP3 lets your email app download messages from the mail server to your computer. Sending mail is SMTP.

68.cue: used only in a corporate environment
68.tip: Home users have antivirus and passwords. Companies add VPNs and IPS.
68.why: VPNs let remote workers reach the company network securely, and an IPS watches network traffic for attacks. Both are business tools. Antivirus, antispyware and passwords are used at home too.

keys.k: protect end devices from becoming infected

69.tip: Antivirus guards the end device itself, like a vaccine for your PC.
69.why: Antivirus is an app on your device that stops malware from infecting it. Filtering network traffic is a firewall's job, and secure tunnels are VPNs.

70.cue: prevent a received IPv4 packet from traveling endlessly

keys.k: decrements the value of the TTL field by 1

70.tip: TTL counts DOWN by 1 at each router. At 0: drop it and send Time Exceeded.
70.why: Every router lowers the TTL by one. When it hits zero the router throws the packet away and tells the sender with an ICMP Time Exceeded message, so loops can't go on forever.

71.tip: 69 = TFTP, the Trivial (simple) FTP over UDP. Regular FTP is 20/21.
71.why: UDP port 69 is used by TFTP, a simple file transfer protocol often used to copy router configs and IOS images.

72.tip: SSH setup: domain name, crypto key generate, transport input ssh on the vty lines.
72.why: The router needs a domain name to build its keys, then RSA keys to encrypt, then the vty lines set to allow SSH only. Allowing Telnet would let unencrypted logins in.

73.tip: MAC = the frame itself: its fields, addresses and FCS. LLC = which protocol is inside.
73.why: The MAC sublayer builds the frame: it marks where the fields start and end and adds the FCS trailer to catch errors. Naming the network protocol is LLC.

74.tip: MAC builds the frame and its FCS trailer. LLC labels the protocol inside.
74.why: The MAC sublayer decides how the frame is laid out and adds the FCS trailer for error checks. Identifying IPv4 or IPv6 and control info are LLC tasks.

75.tip: MAC deals with the media: speeds, fiber vs copper, and CSMA/CD.
75.why: The MAC sublayer talks to the physical media, so it handles different media types and speeds and runs CSMA/CD on old shared half-duplex links. Talking to upper software is LLC.

76.tip: MAC marks the frame's fields and adds the FCS. LLC talks to the upper layers.
76.why: The MAC sublayer marks where frame fields begin so nodes stay in sync, and adds the FCS trailer to detect errors. Naming the network protocol and talking to software are LLC.

keys.k: applies source and destination MAC addresses

77.tip: MAC sublayer = MAC addresses. The name gives it away.
77.why: The MAC sublayer adds the source and destination MAC addresses and marks the frame fields. Identifying the network protocol and adding control info are LLC tasks.

keys.k: all IPv6 configured routers on the local link

78.tip: FF02::1 = all nodes, FF02::2 = all routers (2 for 'routers too').
78.why: FF02 is a link-local multicast. ::1 means every IPv6 device on the link, and ::2 means only the routers on the link.

79.cue: three parts of an IPv6 global unicast address
79.tip: GUA = Prefix + Subnet + Interface. IPv6 has no broadcast and no subnet mask, just a prefix length.
79.why: A global unicast address is the global routing prefix from the ISP, a subnet ID chosen by the site, and an interface ID for the device. IPv6 has no broadcast address.

80.cue: areas of concern, building a wireless network
80.tip: Wireless worries: ICS = Interference, Coverage, Security.
80.why: Radio signals can be disrupted by other devices, can be picked up by outsiders, and only reach so far. So interference, security and coverage must be planned.

81.cue: test whether the banner is properly configured
81.tip: Banner shows at login. Log out of privileged EXEC, press Enter, and see it. No reboot needed.
81.why: The MOTD banner appears when you start a new session. Exiting privileged EXEC mode and pressing Enter brings back the login screen, showing the banner right away without rebooting.

82.cue: contention-based access on a wireless network
82.tip: Wireless AVOIDS collisions (CA). Old wired Ethernet DETECTS them (CD).
82.why: Wireless devices can't hear collisions while sending, so they try to avoid them with CSMA/CA. CSMA/CD is for old half-duplex wired Ethernet.

83.cue: function of the data link layer

keys.k: exchange of frames over a common local media

83.tip: Data link = frames on the local link. End-to-end is transport or network.
83.why: The data link layer puts packets into frames and moves them across one local link or medium. Delivery between hosts or applications is done by higher layers.

84.cue: purpose of the TCP sliding window
84.tip: Sliding window = flow control: the receiver says 'slow down'.
84.why: The window size tells the sender how much it can send before waiting. A receiver that is overwhelmed shrinks the window so the sender slows down.

85.tip: Spyware spies: it collects info about you.
85.why: Spyware hides on your device and gathers information about you, such as what you type or which sites you visit, and sends it to someone else.

86.cue: drops frames that fail the FCS check
86.tip: Store-and-forward stores the whole frame, so it can check the FCS before sending.
86.why: A store-and-forward switch receives the whole frame first and checks the FCS at the end. Bad frames get dropped. Cut-through starts sending before the FCS arrives.

87.why: IPv6 link-local addresses always start in FE80::/10 and only work on the local link. FF00::/8 is multicast, and FEC0 is an old site-local range.

keys.k: data transfers between a client and a file server

88.tip: FTP = File Transfer Protocol: moving files to and from a file server.
88.why: FTP is used to upload and download files between a client and a file server.

89.tip: To reach a website by name you need DNS (name to IP) and a gateway (way out).
89.why: The host needs a DNS server to turn www.cisco.com into an IP address and a default gateway to reach a remote network. Source port and MAC are set automatically.

90.cue: advantage or a disadvantage, NAT for IPv4

keys.k: problems for some applications that require end-to-end connectivity
slow down the IPv4 address depletion

90.tip: NAT: plus = saves IPv4 addresses. Minus = breaks end-to-end apps.
90.why: NAT lets many private devices share one public address, saving IPv4 addresses. But it changes addresses in packets, which breaks apps that need a direct end-to-end connection.

91.tip: EUI-64: split the MAC, put FFFE in the middle, flip the 7th bit (1C becomes 1E).
91.why: EUI-64 inserts FFFE in the middle of the MAC and flips the 7th bit. 1C is 0001 1100, flipping that bit gives 0001 1110 = 1E, so the ID is 1E6F:65FF:FEC2:BDF8.

92.cue: PC1 issues an ARP request, send a packet to PC2

keys.k: PC2 will send an ARP reply with the PC2 MAC address

92.tip: Only the owner of the IP answers ARP. Switches just pass the broadcast along.
92.why: PC2 is on the same LAN as PC1, so the ARP broadcast reaches it and PC2 replies with its own MAC. Switches don't answer ARP, and the router only answers for its own IP.

93.tip: BOOTP = boot protocol, the old grandparent of DHCP for diskless PCs.
93.why: BOOTP is an old protocol that let computers without a disk learn their IP address at startup. DHCP later replaced it.

94.tip: Adware watches what you like so it can show you ads.
94.why: Adware is installed on your device and tracks your habits to show you targeted ads. That makes it a kind of software that collects information about you.

95.cue: error threshold, which switching method will the switch revert
95.tip: Too many errors? Go back to the safe one: store-and-forward checks every frame.
95.why: Cut-through is fast but passes bad frames. When errors pass the set limit, the switch changes to store-and-forward so it can check and drop damaged frames.

96.cue: primary responsibilities of the Ethernet MAC sublayer
96.tip: MAC's two big jobs: wrap the data (encapsulation) and get onto the wire (media access).
96.why: The MAC sublayer wraps packets into frames with addresses and an FCS, and controls when the device can put frames on the media. Logical addressing is Layer 3.

97.tip: Vlan1 has an IP = SVI set = remote management. Only Fa0/1 is up = one device.
97.why: Vlan1, the default SVI, has an IP address and is up, so you can manage the switch remotely. Only Fa0/1 is up/up, which means one device is plugged in.

98.tip: /64 = the first 4 groups. Keep them, zero the rest.
98.why: A /64 prefix is the first four 16-bit groups: 2001:DA48:FC5:A4. The rest is the interface ID, so the subnet is 2001:DA48:FC5:A4::/64.

99.cue: part of a normal network behavior
99.tip: Baseline = what normal looks like. Compare today against it.
99.why: A baseline records how the network normally performs at different times. Comparing the slow periods to it shows whether the delays are normal or a real problem.

keys.k: stored in router or switch configuration files

100.tip: It hides passwords in the config file from shoulder surfers. It doesn't encrypt network traffic.
100.why: This command scrambles plain text passwords in the configuration so someone viewing the config can't read them. It does nothing for passwords sent over the network.

101.cue: comparison of IPv4 and IPv6 packet headers

keys.k: Source Address field name from IPv4 is kept

101.tip: IPv6 keeps Version, Source and Destination. TTL becomes Hop Limit. Checksum is gone.
101.why: IPv6 keeps the Source Address field name, and replaces TTL with Hop Limit, which does the same job. Version is still there, and the Header Checksum was removed.

102.cue: same network mask, IP phones 22, PCs 20
102.tip: Size for the biggest: 22 + 2 = 24, round up to 32. /27 = .224.
102.why: With one mask for all, it must fit the largest network: 22 phones. A /27 (255.255.255.224) gives 30 usable hosts. A /28 gives only 14.

103.tip: Identity theft = using someone else's login.
103.why: Identity theft is when an attacker uses stolen usernames, passwords or other credentials to pretend to be you and get private data.

104.why: Only a /24 (255.255.255.0) is big enough: 254 usable hosts. A /25 would only give 126.

105.cue: standards for constructing and installing cabling
105.tip: Cabling standards cover Length, Pinouts, Connectors. Not price or color.
105.why: Cabling standards set how long a cable can be, which wire goes to which pin, and which connectors to use. Cost and connector color are not part of the standard.

106.tip: Keep the twists right up to the connector: untwist as little as possible.
106.why: When the wire pairs are untwisted too far from the connector, they lose their crosstalk protection and the link gets noisy. Untwist only about 1.25 cm (half an inch).

107.why: TCP port 143 is the well-known port for IMAP, used to read email that stays on the server.

108.cue: characteristics shared by TCP and UDP
108.tip: Both use ports and checksums. Only TCP has handshakes and windows.
108.why: Both TCP and UDP use port numbers to reach the right app and a checksum to catch errors. The 3-way handshake and window size are TCP only, and connectionless is UDP only.

109.tip: 10 hosts needs /28 (14 hosts). /28 blocks start on multiples of 16: 208, 224, 240.
109.why: A /28 gives 14 usable hosts, enough for 10. Addresses up to .199 are taken by the /26 and /29, so free /28 blocks start at .208 and .224. .200 is not a /28 boundary.

110.tip: FTP uses 21 for control and 20 for data.
110.why: TCP port 21 is the FTP control port, where the client sends commands to the file server.

111.cue: attribute of a NIC, data link layer
111.tip: Layer 2 = MAC address. Layer 3 = IP address. Layer 1 = cables and ports.
111.why: The MAC address burned into the NIC is a Layer 2 (data link) address. The IP address is Layer 3, and the cable and RJ-45 port are Layer 1.

112.why: A /28 (255.255.255.240) has 16 addresses, 14 usable, which fits 10 devices. A /29 only has 6 usable.

keys.k: twisting the wires together into pairs

113.tip: UTP = Unshielded TWISTED Pair. The twist is the protection.
113.why: Twisting each pair makes the noise picked up by the two wires cancel out, which cuts crosstalk. UTP has no foil shield.

114.tip: /29 = blocks of 8. Fifth subnet (start at zero) = 4 x 8 = .32. First host .33, last host .38.
114.why: /29 subnets go .0, .8, .16, .24, .32. The fifth is .32, broadcast .39. The router gets the first host .33 and the server the last host .38, with mask 255.255.255.248.

115.cue: Which network hosts will receive the ARP request sent by host A

keys.k: only hosts B, C, and router R1

115.tip: ARP is a broadcast: it reaches everyone on A's LAN, but routers stop it.
115.why: The ARP broadcast floods out every port of the switch, so B, C and R1 get it. R1 does not forward broadcasts, so D on the other LAN never sees it.

116.cue: total host addresses are unused across all four subnets
116.why: Each /26 gives 62 usable addresses, so 248 total. The LANs need 30 and 14, and each serial link needs 2, for 48 used. 248 minus 48 leaves 200 unused.

117.tip: 22 = SSH, 23 = Telnet. SSH is one less and secure.
117.why: TCP port 22 belongs to SSH, the encrypted way to log in to a device remotely.

118.tip: IPS = Intrusion Prevention: spots and stops attacks as they spread.
118.why: An intrusion prevention system watches traffic, recognizes attacks like fast-spreading worms, and blocks them. Filtering by address alone is an ACL or firewall.

119.tip: DHCP = Dynamic Host Configuration: hands out IP addresses automatically.
119.why: DHCP gives devices an IP address, mask, gateway and DNS server automatically, so you don't have to type them in by hand.

120.cue: Which network devices will receive the ARP request sent by host A

keys.k: only hosts B, C, and router R1

120.tip: Broadcasts stay inside the LAN. Everyone on A's switch hears it, routers don't pass it on.
120.why: Host A broadcasts the ARP request for its gateway. The switch floods it to B, C and R1. R1 never forwards broadcasts, so D on the far LAN doesn't get it.

121.tip: Zigbee = tiny IoT gadgets sipping power. Wi-Fi and WiMAX are for speed.
121.why: Zigbee is made for IoT devices like sensors that send small bits of data and must run for a long time on little power.

122.cue: resolution of Layer 3 addresses to Layer 2 MAC addresses
122.tip: IPv6 ARP = NS asks, NA answers. Router messages are for gateways, not MACs.
122.why: IPv6 has no ARP. A device sends a Neighbor Solicitation to ask for a MAC address, and the owner answers with a Neighbor Advertisement. Both must be allowed through the ACL.

123.cue: SLAAC, before it can begin to use this IPv6 address
123.tip: DAD = Duplicate Address Detection: ask 'is anyone using this?' with an NS first.
123.why: Before using a new address, the device does Duplicate Address Detection: it sends a Neighbor Solicitation for its own address. If nobody answers, the address is free to use.

124.cue: ping to the default gateway failed, outside host successful
124.tip: If traffic goes THROUGH the gateway fine, the gateway works. It just won't answer pings itself.
124.why: The ping to the outside host worked, so the gateway is up and routing. It must be set to ignore pings sent to itself, for example by a security rule or ACL.

125.why: The interface ID uses the last 64 bits, so you can subnet from /56 to /64. That's 8 bits, and 2 to the power of 8 is 256 subnets.

126.why: A /26 (255.255.255.192) has 64 addresses, 62 usable, which fits 40 devices. A /27 has only 30 usable.

127.cue: host A sends an IP packet to host B, destination address in the frame
127.tip: Remote host? The frame goes to your gateway's MAC. The IP stays the final host.
127.why: B is on another network, so A sends the frame to its default gateway, R2's interface with MAC BB:BB:BB:BB:BB:BB. The frame destination is a MAC, not an IP address.

keys.k: without requiring investment in new infrastructure

128.tip: Cloud = rent instead of buy. No new servers, staff or software.
128.why: With cloud computing you use someone else's servers and apps over the internet, so you can grow without buying equipment or hiring more staff. Smart appliances are IoT, personal tools are BYOD.

129.cue: MAC and IP addresses during data transmission, NAT is not involved

keys.k: Destination IP addresses in a packet header remain constant
local significance and change every time

129.tip: IP = the final address on the envelope, never changes. MAC = the next stop, changes at every router.
129.why: Without NAT, the destination IP stays the same from start to finish. MAC addresses only matter on one LAN, so each router puts on new source and destination MACs.

130.cue: main characteristic of the data link layer
130.tip: Data link hides the cable type from IP. IP doesn't care if it's Wi-Fi or copper.
130.why: The data link layer prepares packets for whatever media is used, so upper layers like IP don't need to know about it. Making signals is the physical layer, choosing paths is the network layer.

131.cue: three characteristics of the CSMA/CD process

keys.k: All of the devices on a segment see data

131.tip: CSMA/CD: listen first, everyone hears everything, after a crash wait a random time.
131.why: On shared Ethernet, all devices hear the traffic, each one listens before sending, and after a collision they wait a random time before trying again. Tokens and priorities are not part of it.

keys.k: saved configuration file in the NVRAM

132.tip: Startup = saved in NVRAM. Running = live in RAM.
132.why: The startup config is the saved configuration stored in NVRAM, used when the device boots. The running config is the active one in RAM.

133.cue: Windows host to display the routing table
133.tip: Windows routes: route print or netstat -r (r for routes). show ip route is Cisco.
133.why: On Windows, both route print and netstat -r show the PC's routing table. show ip route only works on Cisco devices, and tracert traces a path.

134.cue: two functions provided by the network layer

keys.k: directing data packets to destination hosts on other networks

134.tip: Network layer = addressing (IP) and routing. Layer 3 does the 'where' and 'how to get there'.
134.why: The network layer gives each device an IP address and moves packets across networks to the right host. Putting data on the media is Layer 1/2, and process-to-process is transport.

135.cue: features of an IPv4 routing table on a router

keys.k: routes derived from the active router interfaces

135.tip: C = connected (from active interfaces), S = static (including the default route).
135.why: A router adds routes for its own active interfaces as C and L. Static routes, including a default static route, show up with code S. Routing tables hold no MAC addresses.

136.cue: features of an IPv4 routing table on a router [Other case]

keys.k: routes derived from the active router interfaces

136.tip: Active interfaces make C routes. Static and default static routes get S.
136.why: Routes for active interfaces are added automatically as connected routes. A default static route appears as an S entry. netstat -r is a PC command, and the table holds no MACs.

137.tip: VPN = a private tunnel through the public internet.
137.why: A VPN builds an encrypted tunnel over the internet, so remote users can safely reach their organization's private network.

138.cue: Layer 2 switch need an IP address
138.tip: A switch moves frames without an IP. The IP is only so YOU can reach it remotely.
138.why: A Layer 2 switch forwards frames using MAC addresses, so it doesn't need an IP to work. You give it one, on the SVI, so you can manage it by Telnet or SSH.

139.cue: HTTP request to a remote web server, frame destination

keys.k: MAC address of the default gateway

139.tip: Remote target: frame to the gateway's MAC, packet to the server's IP.
139.why: Frames only travel on the local LAN. To reach a remote server, the host sends the frame to its default gateway, so the destination MAC is the gateway's MAC.

140.cue: advantage to using a protocol defined by an open standard
140.tip: Open = anyone can build it = more vendors to choose from.
140.why: Open standards can be used by any vendor, so products from different companies work together. That gives buyers more choices and keeps prices fair.

141.cue: function of TCP or UDP, source PC to a destination server

keys.k: source port field identifies the running application
UDP segments are encapsulated within IP packets
UDP destination port number identifies the application

141.tip: Ports name APPS, not hosts. Source port = app on the PC, destination port = service on the server.
141.why: The source port tells the PC which app gets the reply, the destination port tells the server which service gets the data, and segments ride inside IP packets. Ports never identify the host.

142.cue: 128.107.0.0/16, maximum number of equal size subnets
142.tip: Size for the largest LAN: 100 hosts + 2 = 102, round up to 128. /25 = .128.
142.why: Every subnet must fit the biggest LAN, which has 100 hosts. A /25 (255.255.255.128) gives 126 usable, and a /26 gives only 62. /25 is the smallest that fits, so you get the most subnets.

143.cue: same subnet mask for three subnetworks at a small site
143.tip: Pick the mask for the biggest group. /28 = .240 gives 14 hosts.
143.why: One mask for all subnets must fit the largest group of devices. A /28 (255.255.255.240) gives 14 usable hosts, which is enough here without wasting addresses like a /24 would.

144.cue: displayed in the output of show ip interface brief
144.tip: Brief = name, IP, status, protocol. No MACs, speeds or descriptions.
144.why: show ip interface brief lists each interface with its IP address, its Status (Layer 1, up or down) and its Protocol (Layer 2). Details like MAC and speed are in show interfaces.

145.cue: web page is taking longer than normal to load
145.tip: Slow somewhere along the way? tracert shows each hop and its delay.
145.why: tracert lists every router on the path and how long each one takes to answer, so you can see where the delay starts. ping only tells you the total time.

146.tip: TTL counts down by 1 at each router hop.
146.why: Each router lowers the Time-to-Live by one. When it reaches zero the packet is dropped, which stops packets from looping forever.

147.cue: issues before implementing fiber optic media
147.tip: Fiber: faster and immune to EMI/RFI, but costly and needs special skills. It's fragile.
147.why: Fiber needs special tools and skills to connect and splice, and it costs more than copper even though it carries more data. It's not affected by EMI or RFI, but it breaks easily.

148.cue: tracert, router stop forwarding the packet
148.tip: tracert raises TTL one step at a time. Each router drops it when TTL hits 0 and reports back.
148.why: tracert sends packets with TTL 1, then 2, and so on. Each router lowers the TTL, and the one where it hits zero drops the packet and sends back Time Exceeded, revealing itself.

149.tip: Worms crawl the network by themselves and eat bandwidth.
149.why: A worm copies itself across the network without help, and all that copying uses up bandwidth and slows the network. A virus needs a user to spread it.

150.cue: Match the description to the IPv6 addressing component

keys.k: assigned by the provider. global routing prefix
host portion of an IPv4 address. interface ID

150.tip: Prefix from the ISP, subnet ID from you, interface ID = the host. No subnet mask in IPv6.
150.why: The ISP gives you the global routing prefix, your organization picks subnet IDs, and the interface ID identifies the device, like the host part in IPv4. Subnet mask is an IPv4 idea.

151.cue: Match the characteristic to the forwarding method
151.tip: Cut-through = fast but sloppy. Store-and-forward = slower but checks everything.
151.why: Cut-through starts sending as soon as it reads the destination MAC, so it's quick but can pass bad or tiny frames. Store-and-forward waits for the whole frame and checks its length and CRC first.

152.cue: Match the application protocols to the correct transport protocols
152.tip: Trivial and quick (TFTP, DHCP) = UDP. Must arrive whole (FTP, HTTP, SMTP) = TCP.
152.why: File transfer, web pages and email must arrive complete, so FTP, HTTP and SMTP use reliable TCP. DHCP and TFTP are simple request and reply protocols that use faster UDP.

153.cue: Match the type of threat with the cause
153.tip: Electrical = power, Hardware = broken gear, Environmental = heat and humidity, Maintenance = sloppy care.
153.why: Power problems like spikes and brownouts are electrical. Damaged devices are hardware threats. Heat, cold and humidity are environmental. Poor handling, missing spares and bad labels are maintenance.

154.cue: Match a statement to the related network model

keys.k: no dedicated server is required peer-to-peer network
background service is required peer-to-peer application

154.tip: P2P network = no server, roles swap per request. P2P app = needs its own interface and background service.
154.why: In a P2P network, no dedicated server is needed and each device is client or server per request. A P2P application, like a file sharing app, needs its own user interface and a background service.

155.cue: Match each type of frame field to its function

keys.k: addressing this field helps to direct the frame
type this field is used by the llc
frame start this field identifies the beginning

155.tip: Start = beginning, Address = where to go, Type = which L3 protocol, Error detection = damaged?
155.why: Frame start marks where the frame begins, addressing steers it to the destination, type tells LLC which Layer 3 protocol is inside, and error detection (FCS) checks for damage.

156.cue: Match the firewall function to the type of threat protection

keys.k: IP or MAC address packet filtering
unsolicited incoming sessions stateful packet inspection

156.tip: Ports = application, addresses = packet, unsolicited = stateful, websites = URL.
156.why: Application filtering blocks by port number, packet filtering by IP or MAC address, stateful inspection blocks incoming sessions nobody asked for, and URL filtering blocks websites.

157.cue: Match the characteristic to the category, IP or MAC

keys.k: OUI and a unique identifier mac address

157.tip: IP: Layer 3, 32 or 128 bits, network + host. MAC: Layer 2, 48 bits, OUI + vendor ID.
157.why: IP addresses sit in the Layer 3 header, are 32 bits (IPv4) or 128 bits (IPv6), and split into network and host parts. MAC addresses are in the Layer 2 header, 48 bits, split into OUI and a unique ID.

158.cue: Match the header field with the appropriate layer of the OSI model
158.tip: MAC, 802.2, FCS = Layer 2. IP, TTL = Layer 3. Ports, ACKs = Layer 4.
158.why: Frame fields like MAC addresses, the 802.2 header and FCS belong to Layer 2. IP addresses and TTL are in the Layer 3 packet. Port numbers and acknowledgment numbers are in the Layer 4 segment.

159.cue: Match each description to its corresponding term

keys.k: encapsulation the process of placing one message format inside another
sizing the process of breaking up a long message
encoding the process of converting information

159.tip: Encapsulation = wrap it, Sizing = chop it, Encoding = convert it.
159.why: Encapsulation puts one message format inside another, like a letter in an envelope. Sizing breaks long messages into pieces. Encoding changes information into a form that can be sent.

160.cue: Match each description with the corresponding TCP mechanism

keys.k: missing segments of data sequence numbers
before transmitting more segments in a session acknowledgment

160.tip: Window = how much at once. Sequence = spot gaps. Retransmit = resend lost. ACK = 'got it, send more'.
160.why: Window size is how many bytes the receiver can take at once. Sequence numbers reveal missing segments. Retransmission resends lost data. The sender waits for acknowledgments before sending more.

161.cue: Match each item to the type of topology diagram

keys.k: location of a desktop pc in a classroom physical topology diagram
ip address of a server logical topology diagram

161.tip: Physical = where things are and how cables run. Logical = addresses and how data flows.
161.why: A physical topology diagram shows real locations of devices and cable paths. A logical topology diagram shows addressing like a server's IP address. USB ports are on neither.

162.cue: Match each description with an appropriate IP address
162.tip: 127 = loopback, 169.254 = link-local, 240 and up = experimental, the rest here = public.
162.why: 127.0.0.1 is loopback to test yourself, 169.254.x.x is link-local when DHCP fails, 240.0.0.0 and above is reserved for experiments, and 198.133.219.2 is a normal public address.

163.cue: satisfy the usable host addressing requirements
163.tip: Biggest network gets the biggest block: 100 = /25, 50 = /26, 25 = /27, 2 = /30.
163.why: Pick the smallest block that fits: A needs 100 hosts (/25 gives 126), B needs 50 (/26 gives 62), C needs 25 (/27 gives 30) and the D link needs 2 (/30 gives 2).

164.cue: Match the network with the correct IP address and prefix
164.tip: Biggest first: 100 hosts /25, 50 hosts /26, 25 hosts /27, 2 hosts /30.
164.why: Network A needs 100 hosts, so a /25 (126 usable) at .0. B needs 50, so a /26 (62) at .128. C needs 25, so a /27 (30) at .192. The 2-host link D gets a /30 at .224.

165.cue: Host B on subnet Teachers transmits a packet to host D
165.tip: Leaving B: MAC to the router's Fa0 (ab), IP to host D (.20.200).
165.why: D is on another subnet, so B sends the frame to the router's Fa0 MAC, 00-00-0c-94-36-ab. The IP addresses stay end to end: source 172.16.10.200 (B), destination 172.16.20.200 (D).

166.tip: RJ-45 = Ethernet, RJ-11 = phone. LC and SC are fiber, BNC is coax.
166.why: Ethernet twisted-pair cable ends in an 8-pin RJ-45 connector. RJ-11 is the smaller phone plug, LC and SC are for fiber, and BNC is for coaxial cable.
